lessons.title: کیوں (kyūṅ) — why
lessons.gloss: why — the k- question word chapter seventeen's family lesson had every chance to include and did not

segments.text: Chapter seventeen gathered Urdu's k- question words and named them a family. One member was left out, and it is the one that asks for a reason.

segments.instruction: the joiner two lessons back, the one that turns — lekin
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the joiner two lessons back, the one that turns — *lekin*]

segments.text: کیوں؟ — kyūṅ? — why?
آپ کیوں نہیں …؟ — āp kyūṅ nahīṅ āye? — why did you not come?
Every letter is one you own: ک، ی، و، and the humming ں of chapter six. It stands where کہاں stands — in front of the verb, not at the front of the sentence, which is where English puts why.

One stem, three questions. It is Sanskrit ka-, the interrogative stem behind Latin quis and quid, and behind English who, what, where and why — the wh- of English and the k- of Urdu are the same ancient consonant, moved apart by one sound change.
کیوں on its own, said flatly, is a complete question, and it is what a child says twenty times a day in either language.

segments.instruction: kyūṅ? — on its own
the three k- words in a row — kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the three k- words in a row — *kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ*]

segments.instruction: āp kyūṅ nahīṅ āye? — why did you not come?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *āp kyūṅ nahīṅ āye?* — why did you not come?]

segments.text: Which stem do کیا، کہاں and کیوں share? (Sanskrit ka-, the interrogative stem.) Which English consonant answers Urdu's k-? (The wh- of who, what, where, why.) And where does کیوں stand in the sentence? (In front of the verb, not at the front.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

lessons.title: کون (kaun) — who
lessons.gloss: who — a word this book has shown twice, glossed in passing, and never taught

segments.text: The chapter-eight writing lesson used a three-letter word to practise the letter و and glossed it in passing. It never became a word you own.

segments.instruction: the question word from the lesson before — kyūṅ
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the question word from the lesson before — *kyūṅ*]

segments.text: یہ کون ہے؟ — yih kaun hai? — who is this?
کون؟ — kaun? — who?
Three letters, all long since taught: ک، و، ن. The و is the same letter chapter eight taught as a vowel, and this word is where you first met it without being told what the word meant.

کون is the fourth of the k- family, from Sanskrit kaḥ punaḥ, "who then," worn to a syllable. It is the direct cousin of English who — the ancient word began with a k-sound, and English wrote it hw- and then wh- while keeping the sound, which is why who still starts with the breath the letter w does not say.
Now the family is whole: کیا what, کہاں where, کیوں why, کون who. Four questions and one stem, and a reader who hears the k- knows a question is coming before the sentence ends.

segments.instruction: kaun? — on its own
yih kaun hai?
and answer it — yih merī māṅ hai
segments.source: [YOU SAY: and answer it — *yih merī māṅ hai*]

segments.instruction: the whole family — kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ, kaun
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the whole family — *kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ, kaun*]

segments.text: How many members does the k- family now have in this book, and what are they? (Four — kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ, kaun.) Which English word is کون's direct cousin? (Who.) And which letter in the middle of it did chapter eight teach? (و.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

lessons.title: کیونکہ (kyūṅki) — because
lessons.gloss: because — the question of the last lesson with one syllable added, and the first way this book can explain anything

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: The question is now askable. The answer is not: nothing in this book can put a reason after a claim.

segments.instruction: the two items before this one — kyūṅ, kaun
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the two items before this one — *kyūṅ*, *kaun*]

segments.text: پانی نہیں ہے کیونکہ … — pānī nahīṅ hai kyūṅki … — there is no water, because …
And over the wellbeing frame of chapter four, whose adjective carries two letters still ahead of you in the script ladder: maiṅ ṭhīk nahīṅ hūṅ kyūṅki …, I am not well, because …
Look at the word and the last lesson is inside it: کیوں plus کہ (ki). Urdu builds because by welding why to that — the language answers its own question in a single word.
Spanish does exactly this: por qué asks, porque answers, and the only difference is a space and an accent. English did it too, in forasmuch as, before the phrase went out of use.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: claim first, reason after

utterances: head word: لیکن. what follows it: an objection.
head word: کیونکہ (kyūṅki). what follows it: a reason.

segments.text: Both stand at the head of the clause they govern, and both come after the claim they attach to. Put them in one sentence and you have the whole shape of an argument: ṭhīk hai, lekin … kyūṅki …

segments.instruction: the question, then the answer word — kyūṅ? … kyūṅki
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the question, then the answer word — *kyūṅ? … kyūṅki*]

segments.instruction: maiṅ ṭhīk nahīṅ hūṅ kyūṅki maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *maiṅ ṭhīk nahīṅ hūṅ kyūṅki maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā*]

segments.instruction: an objection and a reason in one breath — ṭhīk hai, lekin … kyūṅki …
segments.source: [YOU SAY: an objection and a reason in one breath — *ṭhīk hai, lekin … kyūṅki …*]

segments.text: What two words is کیونکہ (kyūṅki) built from? (کیوں, why, and کہ, that.) Which Spanish pair is built the same way? (Por qué and porque.) And which comes first, the claim or the reason? (The claim — the reason follows it.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

lessons.title: کہ (ki) — that
lessons.gloss: that — two letters that hang a whole sentence off a verb, and the thing standing between سوچنا and an opinion

segments.text: sochnā, "to think," has been in this book since chapter seven, and in all that time nobody has been able to say what they think.

segments.instruction: the reason word from the lesson before, and the two words inside it — kyūṅki
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the reason word from the lesson before, and the two words inside it — *kyūṅki*]

segments.text: … کہ یہ پانی ہے — maiṅ sochtā hūṅ ki yih pānī hai — I think that this is water.
The verb in front of کہ (ki) is sochtā, whose che and te are still ahead of you in the script ladder, so the frame is printed in romanization and the clause کہ (ki) introduces is printed whole.

کہ does one job: it takes a whole sentence and makes it the object of a verb of thinking, knowing or saying. Everything before it is the frame; everything after it is the thought, in exactly the order it would have had standing alone.
Two letters, both yours — ک and ہ — and you have been reading them together since the last lesson, welded onto کیوں.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what English drops and Urdu keeps

segments.text: English can leave that out — I think this is right is ordinary English. Urdu cannot: کہ (ki) is obligatory, and a sentence built without it is not merely informal, it is wrong.

The word is Persian ki, borrowed rather than inherited — which is why it sits unstressed and one-shaped wherever it lands. Compare کہاں, where, which begins with the same two letters and is a completely different word from a different source: one of the places Urdu's two ancestries look identical on the page.

segments.instruction: maiṅ sochtā hūṅ ki yih ṭhīk hai
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *maiṅ sochtā hūṅ ki yih ṭhīk hai*]

segments.instruction: maiṅ samajhtā hūṅ ki …
an opinion, then an objection to it — maiṅ sochtā hūṅ ki ṭhīk hai, lekin …
segments.source: [YOU SAY: an opinion, then an objection to it — *maiṅ sochtā hūṅ ki ṭhīk hai, lekin …*]

segments.text: What does کہ attach to the verb in front of it? (A whole sentence, as its object.) Can it be left out, the way English leaves out that? (No — Urdu requires it.) And where have you already read these two letters? (Inside کیونکہ (kyūṅki).)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.

lessons.title: کے لیے (ke liye) — for, in order to
lessons.gloss: for, in order to — the postposition that turns any of this book's fourteen infinitives into a purpose

segments.text: Chapter six taught the -نا ending every Urdu verb wears in the dictionary. Fourteen verbs have that ending and not one of them has ever been the reason for anything.

segments.instruction: the complementiser from the lesson before — ki
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: the complementiser from the lesson before — *ki*]

blocks.title: You'll want to know: کے لیے

segments.text: پانی کے لیے — pānī ke liye — for water.
paṛhne ke liye — in order to read.

Two words, five letters, and every one of them long since yours: ک، ے، ل، ی، ے. Put it after a noun and it means for. Put it after a verb and it means in order to — and the verb's -نا becomes -نے first, which is the one change the construction asks for.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two ways to say why

utterances: shape: کیونکہ (kyūṅki) + a whole clause. says: because something is so.
shape: verb + کے لیے (ke liye). says: in order to do something.

segments.text: The first gives a cause, the second gives a purpose, and a learner who owns both can answer kyūṅ? two different ways.

لیے is the perfective participle of لینا, "to take," which chapter eight taught. Urdu builds for out of having taken: a purpose is what the action was taken for. English went the other way and built for out of a word for before.

segments.instruction: pānī ke liye
the infinitive, then the purpose — paṛhnā … paṛhne ke liye
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the infinitive, then the purpose — *paṛhnā … paṛhne ke liye*]

segments.instruction: samajhne ke liye — in order to understand
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *samajhne ke liye* — in order to understand]

segments.instruction: both answers to kyūṅ? — kyūṅki … and … ke liye
segments.source: [YOU SAY: both answers to *kyūṅ?* — *kyūṅki …* and *… ke liye*]

segments.text: What does the infinitive's -نا become before کے لیے (ke liye)? (-نے.) Which verb is لیے built on? (لینا, to take — chapter eight.) And what does کے لیے (ke liye) give that کیونکہ (kyūṅki) does not? (A purpose, rather than a cause.)
Source: Unicode Arabic chart.
